bio.en: Dharmesh Shah is the co-founder and CTO of HubSpot, the publicly traded CRM and inbound-marketing platform that grew from a scrappy SMB-focused startup into a multi-billion-dollar company serving hundreds of thousands of businesses.
bio.zh: Dharmesh Shah 是 HubSpot 的联合创始人兼 CTO。HubSpot 是一家上市的 CRM 与集客营销平台，从一家专注中小企业的草根创业公司，成长为服务数十万家企业、市值数十亿美元的公司。

summary.en: Dharmesh Shah shares the contrarian, systems-minded playbook behind building HubSpot. He argues most "first principles" thinking is misused, and instead favors "high-conviction, low-consensus bets" — decisions like focusing on SMBs when everyone said it was impossible. A recurring theme is fighting complexity: he treats simplicity as something you must actively fight for, because entropy (the second law of thermodynamics) always increases in companies and code. He explains HubSpot's "flash tags" (FYI → suggestion → recommendation → plea) for calibrated communication, the "debate, decide, unite" decision model, and an Excel-style framework for evaluating ideas by potential, probability, passion, and prowess. On culture, his breakthrough insight is that "culture is a product" you build for your team and must iterate like software rather than freeze. He closes with why AI excites him more than any prior platform shift — it delivers cognition at scale and moves software from imperative to declarative interfaces.
summary.zh: Dharmesh Shah 分享了打造 HubSpot 那套反共识、系统化思维的玩法。他认为大多数"第一性原理"是被误用的，转而推崇"高信念、低共识的赌注"——比如在所有人都说不可能时，押注中小企业市场。贯穿全场的主题是"对抗复杂度"：他把"简单"当作必须主动去争取的东西，因为熵（热力学第二定律）在公司与代码里只会不断增加。他讲解了 HubSpot 用于精准沟通的"闪电标签"（FYI → 建议 → 推荐 → 恳求）、"辩论、决定、团结"的决策模型，以及用潜力、概率、热情、实力来给点子打分的 Excel 式框架。谈到文化，他最突破的洞见是"文化即产品"——你是为团队造产品，必须像软件一样迭代，而不是冻结它。最后他讲为何 AI 比以往任何平台变革都让他兴奋：它带来"规模化的认知"，把软件从命令式界面推向声明式界面。

(00:07:33): But as I came to this realization that I was not going to be able to talk my way out of it, and I saw where this was headed, I'm like, "Okay, this is something I'm going to have to actually learn, because I can't delegate it, can't talk my way out of it." And that's true. That exists, but the way I think about it is talent basically controls the slope of the curve, but most things are actually acquirable skills. So for instance, if you have a talent for music, let's say, you might learn music faster than someone else and your ceiling may be higher, but does not mean that other people can't learn music, right? (00:08:18): It's like an acquirable skill. That's lesson number one. And lesson number two is that there is a process, and this is the engineer in me of just kind of functional decomposition of a problem to say, " Okay, in order for me to be a pretty good public speaker, what are the underlying sub-skills required in order to accomplish that? Okay, skill number one, you have to be able to stand up on stage and not pass out." That's kind the bare minimum. And so what I did over the years is to say, "Okay, I'm going to functionally decompose this skill of public speaking in front of," what I call high-stakes speaking. I've got to actually hold the audience's attention. That's part of success. So it doesn't matter what the message is, nothing else will matter if I lose their attention, which is increasingly easy to do now in kind of short attention span society. (00:09:06): And every year I will pick a different part of the public speaking skill set and say, "Oh, I want to learn about slide design and visual expression," Not the actual design. I'm not a designer. But then the one thing that I came up that has had the most impact is humor. Then you break that skill down just like the engineer would do. It's like, okay, well there's humor writing, there's humor, execution on stage, whatever. There's standup comedy. There's like, okay, so how do you put all these pieces together? And along that journey, I came up with this... and I've always had this, I'm a very data-driven, quant based person. It's like, "Okay, well, how will I know whether something is actually funny enough or not, whether I'm losing the attention or not?" And so in preparation for one of these high stakes keynotes that I do every year, I will have my talk, I will do practice runs. (00:09:57): I will have increasingly larger actual live audiences that I will practice it in front of. I will record those talks, everything so far. Nothing unusual yet. I will have the talks transcribed. I have custom software that I've written that will say, "Okay, here are the points at which the audience laughed." Actually audibly laughed. That's the only way it counts. And this actually... and it comes down to this metric that standup comedians use called LPM laughs per minute. And there's actually a benchmark that you can say, "Oh, well..." And standup comedians have a very, very high LPM. Business talks have a very, very low LPM. The most popular Ted talks there's a high strong correlation between the most popular Ted talks and high. So I have a goal, look, I'm going to have a minimum I want to improve. And so I have software that will calculate the laughs per minute. (00:10:48): And so then you learn these little kind of tools of the tricks of the trades. It's like, okay, if you're solving literally for that ratio of laughs per minute, there are two ways to improve it. One is to add more laughs. Two is to decrease the number of words between laughs, right? So one of the things a software measures, it gives me a visual map. It's like, here's the entire talk broken down with little square per minute of talk, or 30 seconds, and it's like, here's what they like. It's like, "Oh, here I went one minute and 17 seconds and nobody laughed." So I have to do one of two things. Shorten that segment if there's nothing funny that can be said without being overt about it, or I have to say, "Okay, I'm going to find something funny to try to inject into this and kind of break it up." (00:11:29): Anyway. And that's a long way of saying if I can get up on a public stage and learn that particular skill, anyone can learn just about anything. It just comes down to practice and measurement and just getting incrementally better over time.
turns.zh: 其实，我从头说起。公开演讲不是我天生就擅长的。所以我们就从这儿开始。可以稍微聊聊文案，还有相关的一些事。我尽量不去做自己不擅长、也不喜欢的事。少数的几个"漏网之鱼"之一，就是作为创始人，在 HubSpot 年度大会（我们的 conference）上我得登台。第一次办的时候，马里奥特酒店里也就 150 人。之后稳步增长，现在现场观众能有 1 万人，线上几十万。（00:07:33）当我意识到我没法靠嘴皮子逃脱这件事、也看清了它往哪发展时，我就想："好吧，这东西我真的得学，因为我没法 deleg 给别人，也没法靠耍嘴皮子躲掉。"所以我非常相信"天赋 vs 技能"这套。大家都懂天赋——有人有音乐天赋，有人有运动天赋，whatever。天赋是存在的，没错。但我看待它的方式是：天赋基本只决定那条曲线的斜率，但大多数事其实都是可以习得的技能。比如你很有音乐天赋，你学音乐可能比别人快、上限可能更高，但这不意味着别人就学不了音乐，对吧？（00:08:18）它是一种可习得的技能。这是第一课。第二课是：凡事都有流程——这是我工程师那一面，把问题做"功能分解"："好，为了成为一个还不错的公开演讲者，需要哪些底层子技能？"第一技能：你能站在台上不晕倒。这是最低底线。所以我这些年的做法是：把这种我称为"高风险演讲"的公开演讲技能做功能分解。我必须真正抓住观众的注意力，这是成功的一部分。所以不管你的信息是什么，一旦我丢了他们的注意力，别的就都不重要了——在这个注意力越来越短的社会，丢注意力越来越容易。（00:09:06）每年我会挑公开演讲技能树里不同的一个部分，说"哦，我想学幻灯片设计和视觉表达"——不是真的设计，我不是设计师。但后来我搞出来的、影响最大的一个，是幽默。然后你像工程师那样把这个技能拆解：有幽默写作、有台上的幽默执行，等等。有单口喜剧。好，那怎么把这些拼起来？在这趟旅程里，我搞出了这个……我一直就是这样的人，非常数据驱动、量化导向。"好，那我怎么知道某样东西够不够好笑、我有没有在丢注意力？"所以在准备每年那场高风险的主题演讲时，我会先把演讲做好，做彩排。（00:09:57）我会找越来越大的真实现场观众来彩排。我会录下那些演讲，到目前为止都正常。我会把演讲转成文字稿。我写了个定制软件，它会说："好，这是观众发笑的各个时间点。"是真正出声笑的那种。那才作数。这就归结到单口喜剧演员用的那个指标，叫 LPM——每分钟笑声次数。而且确实有基准：单口喜剧演员的 LPM 非常高，商业演讲的 LPM 非常低。最火的那些 TED 演讲，高 LPM 和受欢迎程度之间有很强的相关性。所以我有个目标——我至少要有所提升。于是我有个软件会算每分钟笑声次数。（00:10:48）然后你就学到了这些行业小技巧。比如，如果你真的是在优化那个"每分钟笑声"的比值，有两种提升方法：一是多加笑声，二是减少两次笑声之间的字数，对吧？软件会给我一张可视化地图：整场演讲被切成每分钟或每 30 秒的小方块，标出哪里他们笑了。"哦，这里我讲了 1 分 17 秒，没人笑。"那我就得做两件事之一：把那段缩短（如果实在没法在不刻意的情况下加笑点），或者我得说"好，我去找点好笑的塞进去，把它打散"。（00:11:29）总之。说这么多就是想讲：如果我都能站上公开舞台、学会那项特定技能，那任何人几乎都能学会任何东西。归根结底就是练习、测量，然后随着时间一点点变好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I feel like I've just learned so much about you and how you think just from that question and how you approach this problem. On this humor piece, I'm curious, any lessons to share on how to be funny?
turns.zh: 哇。光从这个问题和你看待这个问题的方式，我就学到了好多关于你、关于你怎么思考的东西。在幽默这块，我好奇，有没有什么关于"怎么变好笑"的心得可以分享？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: One of the kind of tricks of the trade in humor, and you learned this particularly in stand-up comedy, but just any comedy. And I just hadn't thought of it this way, is that... and this is very tactical, but it works and it's a very easy thing to apply. So let's say you're looking at... and most of us, we're not stand-up comedians. We're not going to tell jokes in a classic sense. (00:12:14): And even stand-up comedians don't tell jokes. They actually have stories and they happen to have a punchline or two. So, two tactical pieces of advice. One is when you're telling the story, whatever the funny bit is, those have to literally be the last words of that particular segment. So once you deliver it, then you have to stop talking. And the reason you have to stop talking is the audience needs about a half a second to react, and then they want the permission to laugh. And if you're continuing to say words, it's going to make them feel awkward and it's going to be less funny. So even if moving a phrase in the sentence that you're about to say, it's like, "Well, that sounds kind weird to put those set of words at the end of the thing." Do it anyway even though it's awkward because it will actually work better. (00:13:00): That's kind of tip number one. Tip number two on LPM generally is that having stories such that you can spend the time setting up the story, but then have multiple funny bits, multiple punchlines, because you've already made the investment. I've said 75 words in order to set up this context, say something funny that's amusing, that's whatever. Say some more things. You already have the... and you'll see the stand-up comedians do this all the time. And then say something else that's funny because a laugh is a laugh. Doesn't really matter that it was still the same story. So leverage the investment you've already made in establishing context and scene, and then just squeeze more humor into the end of it in punctuated fashion.
turns.zh: 幽默这个行当有个小技巧——你在单口喜剧里尤其能学到，其实任何喜剧都行。我之前从没这么想过：这非常实操，但管用，而且很容易应用。我们大多数人不是单口喜剧演员，也不会按经典意义"讲段子"。（00:12:14）连单口喜剧演员都不"讲段子"，他们其实是有故事，碰巧带一两个包袱。所以两条实操建议。第一：你讲故事时，那个好笑的点，必须 literally 是那一段的最后一句话。所以你抖出来之后，就得闭嘴。你得闭嘴的原因是，观众需要大约半秒钟去反应，然后他们才"获准"笑出来。如果你还继续说话，会让他们觉得尴尬，也就会更不好笑。所以即使为了把那组词挪到段尾，句子听起来有点怪，也照做——尽管别扭，但它确实更好使。（00:13:00）这是小贴士一。关于 LPM 的小贴士二：用故事。你可以花时间铺垫故事，但然后要塞进多个好笑的点、多个包袱，因为铺垫的"投资"你已经花出去了。我讲了 75 个词来建立这个语境，说点好笑的、逗乐的，whatever。再讲点别的。你已经有了……你会看到单口喜剧演员一直这么干。然后再说点好笑的，因为笑就是笑，管它还是不是同一个故事。所以，利用你已经花在建立语境和场景上的投资，然后在结尾用"标点式"的方式多挤一点幽默进去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like the entire podcast could just be this one thread, but I need to move on to other topics. (00:13:42): One quick question. So you said ideal laughs for a minute is two to three-ish? Is that what you said?
turns.zh: 我感觉整期播客光聊这一条线就够了，但我得往下走别的主题了。（00:13:42）一个快速问题。你说理想的每分钟笑声是两到三次左右？你是这么说的吗？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: Yeah, two plus is hard for a business talk because stand-up comedians, the reason they can do it is that's all they're really solving for is LPM. In business talks, you actually have another agenda other than just being entertaining. You actually have a message. You're trying to promote something. Promote an idea, promote a product. So anyway, in my mind, for most normal circumstance, even if you can get above a one, 1.2, 25, you're in the top decile in terms of top, generally given by non-professionals.
turns.zh: 对。"两次以上"对商业演讲很难，因为单口喜剧演员能做到，是因为他们真正在优化的就只有 LPM。商业演讲里你其实另有议程，不只是逗乐。你是有信息的——你想推广某个东西，推广一个想法、一个产品。所以总之，在我看，大多数正常情况，哪怕你能到 1 以上、1.2、1.25，你就已经排在非专业人士给出的演讲的前 10% 了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, this is incredible. So after every talk, you run this transcript and audio through your program to see how you did.
turns.zh: 哇，这太了不起了。所以每场演讲后，你都把文字稿和音频跑一遍你的程序，看自己表现如何。

turns.en: Yes, yes.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And are you ever going to publish and release this program? Because that sounds really cool.
turns.zh: 那你打算把这个程序发布出来吗？听起来真的酷。

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: I have this notion of what I call SoloWare. And SoloWare is exactly what it sounds like. It's software built for exactly one person, and in my case, that one person is me. And so I've been doing this thing for 30 years right now. I just build things that I would myself find useful. And the nice thing about Solo, one of the many nice things about it is that the UI is only for one person. You don't have to do a whole lot of testing because it only needs to work for one person. And the most important thing is that because it's only for one person, if it stops bringing utility, you can just turn it off. You can just stop using it. Versus if you have users, even 10 users, and you put it out there and then people would be disappointed if you took it down for whatever reason, that's kind of hard. (00:15:10): So anyway, that's the calculus I go through, "Is this useful enough to enough people where it's worth the calories of making it non-solo ware, making it even micro-ware?" I just made that up, but yeah.
turns.zh: 我有个概念，叫 SoloWare（独用软件）。顾名思义：它是为恰好一个人打造的软件，而对我而言，那个人就是我自己。我这么干了快 30 年了——我只做我自己会觉得有用的东西。Solo 的好处之一（也是诸多好处之一）是 UI 只给一个人用。你不用做大量测试，因为它只需对一个人管用。最重要的是，因为它只给一个人用，一旦它不再带来价值，你可以直接关掉、直接不用。而如果你有用户，哪怕 10 个，你把它放出去了，然后不管什么原因你下架，人们会失望，那就很难收场。（00:15:10）所以总之，我会做这笔账："它对足够多的人有用到，值得我花力气把它变成非独用软件、甚至变成微软件吗？"这个词是我刚编的，不过嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Okay. Let's see how the YouTube comments react and how many people would want this and slash pay for it. (00:15:28): Let me go in a slightly different direction. We talked about how you have no direct reports, you've never had any direct reports? I know that's somewhat related to a piece of advice you often share, which is to lean into your strengths and to not do things that you're not amazing yet. So can you just talk about why this is the case? Why don't you have any reports? And then I think this idea of just strengths and the importance focusing on strengths.
turns.zh: 哇。好。咱们看看 YouTube 评论怎么反应、有多少人想要这个、甚至愿意付费。（00:15:28）我换个方向。我们聊了你没有任何直接下属，你从来没过直接下属？我知道这和你常分享的一条建议有点关系：发挥你的优势，别做你还不擅长的事。所以你能讲讲为什么是这样吗？为什么你没有下属？然后我也想聊这个"优势"的想法，以及聚焦优势的重要性。

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: Yeah. I'll tell you the quick story as to how this came about. My co-founder and I had the founding meeting for HubSpot. This is the week where we've decided we're going to do this, and then we have this list of questions or topics for the founders discussion. One of them, and I think I've published a list, these are the questions all co-founders should ask each other in that kind of early period. One of the ones it's like, okay, well who's going to be CEO? This was an easy one because I had been CEO twice before and had figured out I'm not that good at it. I actually suck at that. And one of the reasons I suck at that is that part of the CEO role is being good at managing people. It's not just about leading and having a vision or whatever. Actually have to do the management as a craft. And so, that part I already had in my head. (00:16:40): I think Brian, my co-founder, already had in his head that with... That's how this... that was a very quick conversation. And in the moment, as soon as I had that win behind me, it's like, "Okay, well I don't want to be CEO." Brian wanted to be CEO because he'd never done it before. I'm like, "okay, that was easy." And then I said, "Oh, and by the way, I don't want to have any direct reports." It just popped into my head as an idea. I had not pre-planned it or anything, and I sprung it on him. (00:17:04): He's like, "Okay, well..." And the reason is because I have learned that I suck at management. I'm a reasonably smart person. I think I could become passively okay at management with some training, with some coaching or whatever. I don't want to spend any years of my life becoming passively okay at something. I would rather take those same calories and take the things that I'm good at that I actually enjoy. And those things are highly correlated. You tend to be good at the things you enjoy. You tend to enjoy the things you're good at. And Brian was like, "Yeah, sure." And then I'm like, "No, no, Brian, you don't understand." Because then I was like, "There's going to be a time in the company." He was like, "Oh, our VP of engineering just quit. Just be interim with something or whatever and have this team report to you until we find.." It's like, "We're going to have those things and you're going to have to promise to me we're not going to do that. We're going to..." It's like I am not going to have direct reports. (00:17:53): And we had that kind of heart to heart conversation, and it was one of the best decisions I've made both for myself and for HubSpot. Had I not made that decision, I'm a startup guy, I don't know that I would've survived at a company at HubSpot scale. And right now I can honestly say I'm having a better time at HubSpot now at 7,000 people than I was having at 70 people. And the reason is, I get all the upside of scale, which is I can make big bets. So we can have long-term things and plans, whatever, and plan for global domination without the downsides of scale, which is, "Oh, you're having to manage all these people and all the kind of mechanics." And that's hard. It's a hard skill to have. (00:18:33): I appreciate other people that have it. I don't. And so I get all the upside with very little of the downside of scale, and that's what kind of keeps me engaged and energized and happy at HubSpot. So I think it's been both productive for HubSpot and good for me.
turns.zh: 好。我跟你讲讲这事儿是怎么来的。我和联合创始人开了 HubSpot 的创立会议。那一周我们决定要干这事，然后有一份创始人之间要聊的问题清单。其中一个——我想我公开过那份清单——是所有联合创始人在早期该互相问的问题。其中一个是：好，谁当 CEO？这个好回答，因为我之前当过两次 CEO，已经知道自己不擅长。我其实是真的不行。我不行的原因之一，是 CEO 这个角色有一部分就是要擅长管人，不只是领导和有愿景什么的，而是真的得把管理当一门手艺来做。所以这点我脑子里早有了。（00:16:40）我想我联合创始人 Brian 脑子里也早有了，所以那是个很快的对话。当下，我刚把"CEO 不成"这件事搞定，就想着"好，那我不当 CEO"。Brian 想当 CEO，因为他从没当过。我想"行，这个简单"。然后我说："哦，对了，我也不想要任何直接下属。"这念头是当场蹦出来的，我没预先计划，直接甩给他。（00:17:04）他说"好，嗯……"原因是我认识到自己管人不行。我是个还算聪明的人，我觉得通过培训辅导，也许能把管理做得"还凑合"。但我不想把生命里的任何几年花在把某件事做得只是还凑合上。我宁愿把同样的精力，花在我擅长、而且真的享受的事上。而这二者高度相关：你往往擅长你喜欢的事，也往往喜欢你擅长的事。Brian 说"行，可以"。然后我说"不不，Brian，你不明白"。因为我说"公司总会有那种时刻"。他说"哦，我们工程 VP 刚辞职，你先临时顶一下，让这个团队先汇报给你，直到我们找到……"我就说"这种事一定会来，你得向我保证我们不会这么干。我们……"就是我不要有直属下属。（00:17:53）我们那次推心置腹地聊了，这对我个人和对 HubSpot 都是我做过最好的决定之一。如果没做这个决定，我一个创业佬，不知道自己能不能在 HubSpot 这种规模的公司活下来。而现在我可以诚实地说，在 7000 人的 HubSpot，我比在 70 人时过得还爽。原因是，我拿到了规模的所有上行好处——我能下大注，能做长期的事和计划，能为"统治全球"做规划——却没有规模的下行坏处，也就是"哦，你得管这么多人、管这一堆机械流程"。那很难，是门难的手艺。（00:18:33）我佩服有这门手艺的人，但我没有。所以我拿到了所有上行好处，却几乎不用承担规模带来的下行，这正是让我在 HubSpot 保持投入、有干劲、开心的原因。所以我觉得这既对 HubSpot 有产出，也对我自己好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that this is an example of how you can build a company the way that you want to build it. You don't have to do it the way everybody else has done. I imagine there's a lot of challenges to this too, but I think it's inspiring to just like, "Hey, I'm going to design a company the way I want to build it."
turns.zh: 我太喜欢了——这正是一个例子，说明你可以按自己想要的方式建公司，不必照别人那套来。我猜这也会带来很多挑战，但我觉得这很鼓舞人："嘿，我要按我想的方式设计公司。"

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: Yeah, it's amazing what you can get away with in terms of shaping the universe to your liking. I think people automatically assume that things have to go a certain way, especially founders and first time founders. (00:19:11): It's like, you should at least try it. It's like, "Okay, well I want to do it..." First of, I'll give you another tactical example. Both my co-founder and I are night people, not morning people. Just happens... I didn't pick him because of that. We learned that later. And so we made it just from the early days of HubSpot in the early years at least, we're like, "No meetings before 11 A.M. Period." So you're welcome to meet amongst yourselves if you choose to do so." But anyway, yeah, it's little things.
turns.zh: 对，你能按自己的喜好"重塑宇宙"到什么程度，真的很惊人。我觉得人们会自动假定事情就得那么走，尤其是创始人和第一次创业的人。（00:19:11）你至少应该试试。比如，我再给你一个实操例子。我和联合创始人都是夜猫子，不是早起型。纯属巧合……我不是因为这个才选他的，是后来才发现的。所以至少在 HubSpot 早些年，我们定下："上午 11 点前不开会。句号。"就这条。后来我们调整了，大概三四年之后，我们说"行，上午 11 点前可以开会了。只是你不能拉任何一个联合创始人进去。所以你们自己要开就开。"但总之，都是些小事。

turns.en: That's an amazing rule. I have a personal rule where I have no meetings before 3:00 P.M. because I don't work anywhere. I can more so create my schedule, but the idea is I create this deep work time in the beginnings of the day.
turns.zh: 这规则太绝了。我有个人的规矩：下午 3 点前不开会，因为我不在任何地方坐班。我更能自己安排日程，但核心是我在每天开头留出这段深度工作时间。

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: I love that. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢了。对。

turns.en: Okay. So you talked about you're a startup guy. At the same time HubSpot is approaching its 10 years of being a public company and I think 18 years since founding.

turns.en: Yup.

turns.en: I'm curious what lessons you've taken from that experience being someone that's clearly startuppy person, being an exec at a very fast growing and large company. And I'm thinking from the perspective of a founder who's maybe thinking about starting a company or starting company, what advice you might have to share for them? And also for people in the exact role today?
turns.zh: 我好奇，作为一个明显很"创业范儿"的人、一家高速成长大公司的 exec，你从这段经历里学到了什么。我是站在一个可能正想创业、或正在创业的创始人的视角，想知道你能分享什么建议？也包括给今天正处在这个角色的人？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: A couple of things. One, since we are publicly traded down, this doesn't get talked about enough. I'm going to go and get this out there and use this as a platform to get this message out, which is I think too many founders, once they get to a... They are very apprehensive of going public and going through the IPO process and being a publicly traded company because they think... I mean, that's like the beginning of the end. "It's going to change everything and my life is going to suck." (00:20:58): And I think they're over indexing on what they think it's like to be a publicly traded company. In my own personal experience, and Brian, my co-founder would attest to this. And yes, there's certainly a tax or things we have to do now as a publicly traded company that we didn't have to do as a privately traded company. But there are actually benefits. For instance, if you kind of venture back in private, let's say, you're sort of at a little bit the whim of the market and how VCs perceive your category and all these things or whatever. And you get, every now and then, when you're out raising a round of capital, you sort of get marked to market. Now here's sort of what the valuation is based on what someone's willing to kind of fund the company at. One of the nicest things, and this is underappreciated, is that we know right now what the market values HubSpot at. I can tell you that any business day of the week. And there's a niceness to that. And that's the other thing I tell folks within the company is that the valuation, which is we're in a relatively efficient market. The public stock market is a relatively efficient by the economic definition of the term, in efficient market. So, the valuation will oscillate around the value. (00:22:04): So, if you focus on creating values, here's what we're actually building, valuation will sometimes be higher than you deserve, sometimes will be lower than you deserve, but over the fullness of time, those two things will move in lockstep, right? That's been demonstrated. That's what happens. That's almost a definition of an efficient market is that information moves essentially, and then the valuation catches up with the actual value. (00:22:25): But here's the other social reason why I think founders should go public, which is... So in HubSpot, and I hadn't thought about this so I'm not going to take credit for being this generous, magnanimous person, is that in our first pre-public years, I think we were eight years old when we went public, we had created roughly a billion dollars in market cap, give or take. We hadn't been a unicorn. So it was slightly below when we went public. So HubSpot was never a unicorn because that's private privately held company, over a billion. (00:22:55): In the subsequent years, we went from a billion dollars in market cap to 30 billion, which is roughly what it is now. That first billion of market cap creation, a very small number of people got to participate in. The rest of the $29 billion in market cap, everyone, every public investor got a chance to participate in. And so I like the idea of, okay, well you believe in your company. There's lots of people that believed in HubSpot. It's nice to let them kind of participate. Our customers, our partners, our well-wishers, and they can sort of now have the upside. And you don't get that in the private markets because it's a very closed... you can't just buy shares in every private company you like. I wish that existed, but it doesn't. So, it's a way to let the market at large participate in your growth earlier.
turns.zh: 几点。第一，既然我们已经上市，这点聊得不够多。我要借这个平台把话说出来：太多创始人一旦到了某个阶段，就对上市、走 IPO 流程、变成上市公司特别畏惧，因为他们觉得……那就像是末日的开始。"一切都要变，我的生活要完蛋了。"（00:20:58）我觉得他们对自己想象中"上市公司是什么样"过度加权了。以我的亲身经历，我联合创始人 Brian 也会作证：没错，作为上市公司，我们确实得多做某些"税"或合规的事，私有阶段不用做。但其实也有好处。比如，回到私有阶段，你多少得看市场脸色，看 VC 怎么看你的赛道，等等。你每次出去融一轮，就会被"按市价标记"一次——估值基于别人愿意投多少钱。而最棒的一点（这点被低估了）是：我们现在确切知道市场对 HubSpot 的估值是多少。一周里随便哪个交易日我都能告诉你。这有种舒坦。我在公司里也跟大家说：估值嘛，我们处在一个相对有效的市场。公开股票市场按经济学定义是相对有效的。所以估值会围绕价值上下波动。（00:22:04）所以，如果你聚焦在"创造价值"——也就是我们真正在搭建的东西——估值有时会比你应得的高、有时比应得的低，但拉长看，这两样会齐步走，对吧？这已被证明。这就是会发生的事。一个有效市场的近乎定义就是：信息先流动，然后估值追上真实价值。（00:22:25）但我之所以觉得创始人该上市，还有个社会层面的理由。在 HubSpot，我之前没想过这个，所以我不会贪功说自己是多么慷慨的人：我们上市前那些年，大概是第八年上市的，那时我们创造了约 10 亿市值的样子，上下浮动。我们没当过独角兽——上市时还略低于。所以 HubSpot 从不是独角兽，因为独角兽是私有、估值超 10 亿的公司。（00:22:55）之后的几年，我们从 10 亿市值长到了 300 亿，大概就是现在的样子。那第一个 10 亿市值的创造，只有极少数人能参与。剩下那 290 亿市值，每个公众投资者都有机会参与。所以我喜欢这个想法：好，你相信自己的公司。有很多人相信 HubSpot。让这些人参与进来挺好的——我们的客户、合作伙伴、支持者，他们现在能分享上行。而私募市场给不了这个，因为它非常封闭……你不能随便买你喜欢的任何私公司的股份。我希望有这东西，但没有。所以，上市是让广大市场更早参与你成长的一种方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about from the perspective of just staying excited and motivated and finding things to take on, is there any lessons there for founders that are, I don't know, at a larger company and just, "Okay, this is going to help me stay excited about what I'm doing"?
turns.zh: 那从"保持兴奋和动力、找到可啃的事"这个角度呢？对一家更大公司的创始人，有没有什么能帮他们"保持对自己在做的事兴奋"的教训？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: Yeah, I think this is... and Bezos exemplifies this, I think the best, which is, just because you're a public company does not mandate that you do certain things. All that's necessary is the kind of transparency that says, "Here's what the company is doing, here's what we're about, here's what we're solving." And he had this with his very first annual shareholders letter, which he obviously writes every year, which is, "This is what Amazon is about, we're solving for the long term or whatever." And he didn't say this in a snarky way. If you reread the letter, but if you read between the lines, it's like, if you don't agree with this approach, you should not buy Amazon shares. It's like, it's a completely optional thing. "You don't have to buy it, but this is the way we're going to run the business." (00:24:39): And he stayed true to that. And you can continue to do that. I'll tell you one quick story. This is once again, the anti-dissuade founders that might be reluctant to go public. So one of the core values at HubSpot that's been part of the culture from the early early days, literally days, is transparency. And so, one of our mechanisms by which we implement transparency is we've had this thing that says all information within HubSpot is equally shared with everyone in the company, period. (00:25:11): Everything. So our balance sheet, what we raised capital at, whether we're going to be able to meet payroll in six weeks, all those things, everything was transparent all the time. And with two exceptions. One is if it was illegal for us to share, let's say if we were looking at some acquisition or whatever and we had non-disclosure or the information was ours, not completely ours to share. And one example of that was salaries. So, we feel that salaries are co-owned both by the company and by that individual. And it's not up to us to share someone's salary if they don't want to do that. Okay. All right. (00:25:45): So, we had that transparency and then as we go public, we have this meeting with our investment bankers and our lawyers. This is in the IPO prep process, and they sit down and as part of this all day meeting, one of the questions is like, "Okay, so who are your designated insiders?"
turns.zh: 对，我觉得这点……贝索斯是这方面最好的典范：你是一家上市公司，并不意味着你被强制必须做某些事。唯一必要的是那种透明度——"这是公司在做的事，这是我们的宗旨，这是我们在解决的问题。"他在第一封年度股东信里就写了这个（他每年都写）："这就是 Amazon 的宗旨，我们为长期而解。"他不是说这话带刺。你重读那封信，但如果你读懂字里行间，那是：如果你不认同这个做法，你就不该买 Amazon 的股票。这完全是可选项。"你不必买，但我们就会这么经营。"（00:24:39）他一直忠于这一点。而你也可以继续这么做。我给你讲个短故事，这也是在"劝退"那些可能对上市犹豫的创始人。HubSpot 的核心价值观之一，从最早最早——literally 头几天——起就是透明度。所以我们落实透明度的机制之一是：HubSpot 内所有信息，与公司里每个人平等共享，句号。（00:25:11）一切。我们的资产负债表、我们融资的价格、六周后我们发不发得出工资，所有这些，一切始终透明。只有两个例外。一是如果分享是违法的，比如我们在看某笔收购，签了保密协议，或者信息不完全是我们的。其中一个例子是薪资。我们认为薪资是公司和个人共同拥有的，如果当事人不愿意，轮不到我们来分享。好，行。（00:25:45）所以，我们有那种透明度。然后当我们上市时，我们要和投资银行家、律师开会——这是 IPO 准备流程的一部分。他们坐下来，在那场一整天的会议里，其中一个问题是："好，那么你们的内部人（designated insiders）是谁？"

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: So who are your designated insiders? Brian nor I had ever taken the company public before, we're like, "We don't know what that is." It's like, "Oh, it's this group of people that will have access to all the financials and will know." And we're like, "Oh, okay, so how long is that list?" And they're like, "Five or six." And so then Brian says, "Seven? Seven?" And they're like, "Yeah, you can do seven." And I say, "Eight? Could you do eight?" And so we discovered through that mathematical induction process, is like, "If it's true for N, is it true for N plus one?" Is that there's no actual legal limit to how many insiders a company can have. (00:26:38): And so we ended up doing, literally the day we went public, is we designated every single employee to be a designated insider. So that allowed us to maintain the transparency thing because there was no rule that said you could only have 5, 6, 10, and there was hundreds of people. And we did not make it optional. We didn't say, "Oh," because there are downsides to being an insider. There's windows within which you can't trade, there's stuff. But we're like, "Okay, well, we believe in transparency. Everyone's going to have access to it, and it's not an opt in kind of thing. You're like, "This is it. We're all in it together."" And we still do this to this day, even at 7,000 people, everybody's an insider, so we can still share all the financials with everyone all the time.
turns.zh: 内部人？Brian 和我都没带公司上过市，我们说"我们不知道那是什么。"他们说"哦，就是那群能接触所有财务数据、会知情的人。"我们就说"哦好，那名单多长？"他们说"五六个"。然后 Brian 说"七个？七个？"他们说"对，七个可以"。我说"八个？能八个吗？"于是我们通过那个"数学归纳法"过程发现："如果对 N 成立，那对 N+1 成立吗？"——原来法律对公司能有多少内部人，并没有实际限制。（00:26:38）所以我们最终的做法是：就在上市那天，我们把每一个员工都指定为内部人。这样我们就能维持那种透明度，因为根本没有"只能有 5、6、10 个"的规定，而我们想覆盖的是几百人。而且我们没把它做成可选项。我们没说"哦"——因为做内部人也有坏处，有不能交易的窗口期之类的。但我们就说"好，我们信透明度。人人都能看，这不是 opt-in 的事。这是板上钉钉的。我们同舟共济。"直到今天我们还这么做，哪怕 7000 人了，人人都是内部人，所以我们随时能把所有财务数据分享给每个人。

I'm curious if there's anything else there of just contrarian ways of running a company. I know there's probably many, but what comes to mind?
turns.zh: 从这对话里我已经感觉到，你有很多反共识的观点。你那种"能不能 10 个、能不能 1000 个"的推极限做法，让我好奇：在"反共识地经营公司"上，还有没有别的什么冒出来的？我知道可能很多，但什么先跳进你脑子？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: So one of the phrases we like to use in our industry overall is this notion of first principles. I don't know who popularized it, but it's used a lot. I'm not going to say something snarky, but I think most of the time first principles is used, it's actually used incorrectly. Because the way first principles is supposed to work, as Elon would probably describe it, is that it's not first principles like first principles of what we believe, these are our core first principles in the company, it's the first principles of the universe. It's not what you believe is true, it's what do we all collectively know to be true to the best of our knowledge? It's science. That's physics. Like the first and second law of thermodynamics, those are first principles. All the layers on top of that are things that you think are true, are your assumptions or the decisions you made, and that's fine. You may have made some decisions. (00:28:23): For instance, transparency is not a first principle, it's a founding principle. It's not everyone should do this, it's a completely core thing. And so yes, I can be a contrarian, but you have to limit the dimensions. So the number of things that you're a contrarian on has to be greater than zero, but not too high. So what I think of is high conviction, low consensus bets. So high conviction is, "We really, really believe this," and low consensus is that most other people don't. And there are other people have phrased this differently. I think Peter Thiel actually says it more simply and elegantly, which is, "You need to be right about something that other people think you're wrong about for a very long time." And you just have to be right. (00:29:09): So one of the early high-conviction decisions we made at HubSpot was that we were going to focus on SMB as our target market. And I'll make a case both for SMB and for having a high conviction bet. It doesn't have to be your target market, but something. Once you make that bet, because it's low consensus, it's going to be hard and necessary for you to have the conviction because everyone disagrees, including your board, including your investors, including potential investors. So we have that for literally all 18 years of HubSpot's history. We have always had the... All during the IPO roadshow, it's like, "Yes, we get that you've on SMB, but so what's the path to the enterprise?" No, you don't understand. This is not a go-to market strategy. This is not like, "Oh, we're going to conquer SMB first," this is not Bowling Pin, this is not Geoffrey Moore, this is a, "We are here for SMB." That's what we're doing. (00:29:58): And so we maintain that conviction for a very long time, and that helps you make other bets that are secondary. But you don't want to reinvent everything. So I'll give you an example of something that we had in the early years of HubSpot that we kind of forwent. So in the early years of HubSpot, we're like, "Okay, we believe in a flat organization." One of the manifestations of that flat organization is we had no titles in the company. Nobody had a title. So even though you had business cards, whatever, we had no titles. If you introduce yourself in a meeting, and we had this up to hundreds of people, when you introduce yourself like, "Oh, I work in product, I work in engineering," whatever, it's not like, "I'm director of X or VP of Y," because that, as a thing, didn't exist. (00:30:41): Then as we scaled, we came to the realization that there's actual value that people ascribe to titles. And the reason they ascribe value to titles is because there are rumors that there's life beyond HubSpot. I couldn't believe it. "What? There's a life out there outside of HubSpot?" It's like, " Yeah, looks like." And then when we go to the Thanksgiving dinner or whatever, and I talk to my aunt, I need some shorthand. It's like, "Oh yeah, I got promoted to director. I got..." Just to show some progression because it's a signaling device. (00:31:11): And in this life beyond HubSpot and outside of HubSpot, it's like, other people are also going to want to know where I was in... It's like, "Okay," and this was the winning argument. I love this argument. Because we had a daylong meeting on talking about this one topic. And the winning argument was, "Dharmesh and Brian, I recognize why we don't have titles. I recognize this." And so they made the case of, "Yeah, there's value. And by virtue of you not giving us titles, that means you're having to compensate us in an economic sense in other ways. So you're losing out because it's like, is that value high enough to not do that?" That's a strong case. (00:31:50): And then we had it down to three choices. We're like, "Okay, well," we could have chosen to just stay firm with still no titles. We could have said, "Okay, we're going to have classic titles." Then I had the option on the table of, "Make up your own title." You can be grand poobah of X, and that can be your... And then we ended up making the decision to go with classic titles because that actually served the need of, there's a benchmark, there's a standard, otherwise it doesn't mean anything. So having made-up titles is pretty much the equivalent of having no titles because they lack any meaning anyway. But that's one of those things that, okay, you iterate, you change things as they go.
turns.zh: 我们整个行业爱用一句话，叫"第一性原理"。我不知道谁把它带火的，但用得很多。我不多嘲讽，但我觉得大多数时候"第一性原理"是被误用的。因为按它本来的意思——大概 Elon 会这么描述——它不是"我们相信的第一性原理、我们公司的核心第一性原理"，而是"宇宙的第一性原理"。不是你认为什么是真的，而是我们集体在所知范围内公认是真的？那是科学，是物理。像热力学第一、第二定律，那才是第一性原理。上面叠的所有层，都是你认为真的东西、是你的假设或你做的决定，那没问题，你可能做过一些决定。（00:28:23）比如，透明度不是第一性原理，它是"创立原则"。不是每个人该这么做，而是对我们来说完全核心的东西。所以，对，我可以是反共识的，但你得限制维度。你反共识的事的数量，必须大于零，但不能太高。所以我思考的是"高信念、低共识的赌注"。高信念就是"我们真的、真的相信这个"，低共识就是大多数别人不信。也有别人用不同的话说过。我觉得 Peter Thiel 说得最简练优雅："你得在某件别人长期认为你错的事上，你是对的。"而你只需要是对的。（00:29:09）HubSpot 早期做的一个高信念决定是：我们要聚焦 SMB（中小企业）作为目标市场。我既为 SMB 辩护，也为"有一个高信念的赌注"辩护。它不一定非得是目标市场，但得有某个东西。一旦你下注，因为它低共识，你就必须、也自然会很有信念——因为所有人都反对，包括你的董事会、你的投资人、潜在投资人。所以我们 HubSpot 整整 18 年历史里都是这样。整个 IPO 路演期间，人家都说"好，我们知道你做 SMB，但通往大企业的路径是什么？"不，你不明白。这不是进入市场策略，不是"哦我们先征服 SMB"，这不是保龄球瓶打法，不是 Geoffrey Moore，而是"我们就是为 SMB 而来的"。这就是我们在做的。（00:29:58）所以我们把那份信念维持了很久，而这帮你去做其他次要的赌注。但你也不想什么都重来。我给你个例子，HubSpot 早年的一个我们后来放弃的东西。早年我们说"好，我们相信扁平组织"。扁平组织的一个体现是公司里没有头衔。没人头衔。所以即使你有名片什么的，我们也没有头衔。如果你在会上自我介绍——我们当时几百人时也这样——你会说"哦，我在产品，我在工程"，而不是"我是 X 的总监、Y 的 VP"，因为那东西根本不存在。（00:30:41）然后随着我们扩张，我们意识到人们对头衔确实赋予价值。他们之所以赋予头衔价值，是因为有传言说"HubSpot 之外还有生活"。我简直不敢相信。"什么？HubSpot 之外还有生活？"就像"对，看起来是。"然后感恩节晚餐什么的，我跟阿姨聊，我需要个 shorthand。"哦对，我升总监了。我……"只是为了显示某种进阶，因为它是一种信号装置。（00:31:11）在这 HubSpot 之外、之外的生活里，别人也会想知道我在……就像"好"，而这就是制胜论点。我爱这个论点。因为我们为这一个话题开了一整天的会。制胜论点是："Dharmesh、Brian，我理解我们为什么没有头衔。我理解。"于是他们立论："对，它有价值。而正因你们不给我们头衔，意味着你们得用别的经济方式补偿我们。所以你们在吃亏，因为——那个价值高到值得这么做吗？"这是个强论点。（00:31:50）然后我们把它收敛到三个选择。我们说"好，我们可以坚持不动、仍然没头衔。我们也可以说"好，我们用经典头衔"。"然后我桌上的选项是"自己编头衔"——你可以当 X 的大 poobah（大佬），那可以是你的……最后我们决定用经典头衔，因为它确实满足了需求：有个基准、有个标准，否则它毫无意义。所以编出来的头衔基本等于没有头衔，反正本来就缺含义。但这就是那种事——好，你迭代，随着发展做调整。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I think there's so much to this, "Let's just try things differently. Okay, that didn't work. Okay. It's fine. We're just going to do what everyone else is doing here." And then often you discover a thing that, "Okay, this is actually better."
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这事儿里门道太多了——"咱们就换种方式试试。哦，没成。没事，这事儿我们就照大家通常的做法来。"然后你常常会发现："哦，这个其实更好。"

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: One of the things that, and this is one of the core... And not everything that we... Obviously not everything was right, but not everything is applicable to other companies. But there are some things that I think are, and one of the things that I think are applicable is just this need to solve for simplicity. It's like the simpler you can make things in the early years, the better off you generally are. And this is going to sound weird, so how we wound up with transparency is not because of some moral, it's like, "Oh, everyone deserved to have this," and this is the truth, so it's not some moral position. It was a, when we hired the first employee, and both Brian and I [inaudible 00:33:54], when we hired the first employee, we had to make the decision, it's like, "Oh, so what files do we give them access to and what..." And so Brian is just like, "All of it. Nothing to hide. Why would we do that?" (00:34:09): And so then we thought out... And then the output of that was like, "Okay, well, A, binary decisions are much easier than non-binary decisions." It's like, "Okay, everything or nothing is much, much simpler." And then it's like, "Okay, well, if it works for Employee Number Three in the company, why wouldn't it work at Four? Why wouldn't it work at Five? Why wouldn't it work at 50?" And we just kept doing it because it's like, "Okay, well, until it breaks, we'll just keep doing that." And this applies to so many different aspects of HubSpot, but as we try to start with the simplest possible thing that might work, and then, if necessary, add the complexity, add the things or whatever. Even our original, this is actually the tactical thing that everyone should take away, especially early-stage startups, very first HubSpot office has exactly four tables because aspirations for growth, because we were in a co-working space, so, we lived in WeWork back in the day, here in Cambridge, Massachusetts. (00:35:04): And so we had four chairs, and the only distinguishing characteristic of the four chairs, there were two chairs that were by the window, two chairs, not by the window. Okay, great. Hire that first employee. Other decision we have to make is like, "Okay, well where do people sit?" And so this one is like, "Well, it feels unfair to us that we would just get the window seats or whatever." It's like, "Okay, we believe in a flat organization, why?" And so what we did is we said, "Oh, we'll just do a lottery." And it's not like, "Oh, whoever pulls the thing gets the window seat." Whoever pulls gets to choose from the remaining seats, because different people ascribe different utility to different seats. It's like maybe you don't want a window seat. Maybe you like the darker corner, whatever it is. (00:35:42): And so we did that with employee number one. Then we did that with employee number two, and we did it every time we hired a new employee, we would do a seat shuffle. We're going to do the lottery, we're going to go down the sequence, and of all the seats, that was the algorithm. And our investors were like, "Oh, that's cute and that's funny. It's not going to work at 15, 20 people. It's not going to work at 50." It worked at 25 worked at 50, worked at 100, worked at 200. We updated the algorithm, we did some local optimizations, which we said, "Oh, there are some groups that should not be next to other groups because engineers like quiet time and salespeople don't, and so we're going to try to optimize a little bit." So it's not completely random anymore. Now it's like within this part of... Well, we still would do it. Then we said, "Okay, we're not going to do it for every hire, we're going to do it every quarter." And that stood, by the way, for hundreds of people, that mechanism still worked. It's like it's... Yeah.
turns.zh: 有一件事——这也是我们核心的……当然不是每件事都对，也不是每件事都适用于别的公司。但有些是适用的，其中我觉得普适的一条，就是这种对"简单"的追求。早年你越能把事情做简单，通常处境就越好。这话听起来怪，我们之所以走向透明，不是出于什么道德感，不是"哦，每个人都该看到这些"，这是实情，所以不是道德立场。而是：当我们雇第一个员工时，Brian 和我（听不清 00:33:54）都得做决定："哦，那我们给他开放哪些文件的权限、哪些……"Brian 就说："全部。没什么好藏的。我们为什么要藏？"（00:34:09）于是我们往外推：二元决策比非二元决策容易得多。"全给"或"全不给"简单多了。然后就想："好，这对公司第 3 号员工管用，凭什么对第 4 号不管用？对第 5 号、第 50 号凭什么不管用？"我们就一直这么做，因为"好，在它出问题之前，我们就一直这么干"。这适用于 HubSpot 的方方面面——我们尽量从"可能管用的最简方案"起步，有必要再加复杂度、加东西。就连我们最初——这其实是个所有人该记下的实操点，尤其早期创业公司——最早的 HubSpot 办公室就正好四张桌子，因为我们有成长野心，当时在共享空间，就在马萨诸塞州剑桥那边的 WeWork 里。（00:35:04）所以就四把椅子，四把里两把靠窗、两把不靠窗。好，雇第一个员工。又一个要做的决定："大家坐哪儿？"我们就想："我们要是把靠窗座位自己占了，感觉不公平。"就像"我们相信扁平组织，对吧？"于是我们说："哦，那就抽签。"不是"谁抽到谁坐窗边"，而是抽到的人从剩下座位里挑——因为不同人对不同座位估值不同，也许你不想坐窗边，也许你喜欢暗一点的角落，随你。（00:35:42）第 1 号员工这么干，第 2 号也这么干，之后每次招新人就重排一次座位：抽签、按序挑，这就是算法。投资人说："哦，挺可爱挺逗的，15 人、20 人就不行了，50 人也不行。"结果 25 人行、50 人行、100 人行、200 人都行。我们升级了算法，做了点本地优化——"哦，有些组不该挨着另一些组，因为工程师要安静、销售不要，所以我们稍微优化一下。"所以不完全随机了。但我们还是照做。后来我们说："好，不每次招人都排，每季度排一次。"这套机制，顺便说，几百人时还管用。就是这么回事。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God.
turns.zh: 我的天。

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: So the moral of the story is, that one decision of simplifying, can you imagine the amount of politics we avoided? In corporate America, the amount of calories spent is like, "Well, your office is bigger than my office. Your desk is one inch higher or one..." Like, "No." It's like all of that just went away by virtue of that one decision. And we don't even know, it's incalculable, honestly, how much grief that saved us. And then there's all other side benefits to it in terms of people getting to know each other better, better chemistry, there's lots of good upside, but just the simplicity is almost always a better answer.
turns.zh: 所以这故事的寓意是：这一个"简化"的决定，你能想象我们因此避开了多少办公室政治吗？在美国企业里，人们耗掉多少精力在"你的办公室比我大、你的桌子高一英寸"这种事上。我们呢？"没有。"就这一个决定，那些全没了。我们甚至算不出来，说真的，它替我们省了多少麻烦。而且还有各种附带好处——大家彼此更熟、化学反应更好，正向收益很多。但光是"简单"这一点，几乎永远是个更好的答案。

The opposite extreme is, you could say, entropy, and someone told me that you have this concept that every leader in every business is fighting the second law of thermodynamics, which I believe is entropy.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢了——你做的事最后总会回到你编的某个算法，或者这种"N+1"的思路："我们就一直做下去，直到出岔子。"太绝了。我已经期待更多这种又好笑又厉害的、你们不一样做事的例子了。你一直在讲"简单"。而它的反面极端，可以说就是熵；有人告诉我，你有个概念：每个生意里的每个领导者，都在跟热力学第二定律作战——我印象里那就是熵。

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: Yeah. Well, the actual law is within a closed system, entropy increases over time.
turns.zh: 对。不过严格说，那条定律是：在封闭系统里，熵随时间增加。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: We don't have to get into the [inaudible 00:37:50] of this.
turns.zh: 这个的（听不清 00:37:50）细节咱们就不深究了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I love this.
turns.zh: 不，我太爱这个了。

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: I'm not a physics guy.
turns.zh: 我可不是搞物理的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, we're getting to the first principles of everything. Talk about that. What does that mean when you... And what does that look like when you're running a business?
turns.zh: 不，我们正聊到万事万物的"第一性原理"。你展开说说。当你……这跟你经营公司具体是什么关系？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: Okay, so in lay person's terms, the second law of thermodynamics, I'm paraphrasing here, is that, "Over time, unless you intervene, everything goes to crap." I'm paraphrasing. Which is, essentially, the amount of disorder and randomness in a system is going to increase over time. You see this like when you break an egg, the molecules don't come together and form an egg. That doesn't happen. It's always the other way around becomes disorderly and more random. That's the second law of thermodynamics. And this happens in companies as well, and it happens in code, almost every level of abstraction, you will see some variation of this. And so the way I think about this is that in the early stages of a company, you're essentially fighting to survive. Just trying not to die. That's the thing. Okay, priority one, don't die. In the second phase of a company, you're trying not to stagnate. But it's like you still want to be able to drive growth and be able to do things like, "Okay, we managed not to die, because stagnation is essentially death, so we're still trying not to die." (00:38:58): But then the third stage is you're fighting complexity. And that's the thing that you will crumble under your own weight over time, absent some external intervention. And you see this happen all the time, and it shows up and manifests in different ways, which is, everything gets more complicated. You need more layers of management, more headcount, more this, more that, more everything. Everything becomes harder. Margins go... It's like just bad things start to happen, you become slower. And that's the eventual... It's a slower death, because you're at more scale now, but it's still eventual death. Complexity does kill companies. Maybe not as quickly as other things, but much more reliably than other things. (00:39:38): And so this is why it's never too early to plant the seeds of simplicity, put them in there, make that part of the culture of the organization. And we have a thing that are part of our culture and guiding principles around what I call "fight for simplicity." It's literally those three words. And the message we're trying to convey is, "Simplicity is worth fighting for." That's thing number one, it's important, but the other one is that it requires fighting for. It does not happen, and it will be a fight, because the universe is working against you. And it will take calories to fight for that simplicity, because everything, even well-intentioned people, will introduce complexity because that's the natural way of the world. We want more tiers in our pricing, we want these knobs and dials in the product, we want these more... It's like all of it tends towards the second law and entropy increases. So anyway.
turns.zh: 好，用大白话讲，热力学第二定律——我这里转述一下——就是："随着时间推移，除非你干预，否则一切都走向完蛋。"我这是转述。本质上就是：系统里的无序和随机程度，会随时间不断增加。你打碎一个鸡蛋，分子不会重新聚成鸡蛋，那不会发生；总是反过来的——变得更无序、更随机。这就是热力学第二定律。公司里也发生，代码里也发生，几乎每一层抽象你都能看到它的某种变体。所以我这么想：公司早期，你本质上是在为活下去而战，就想着别死。对，第一优先是别死。第二阶段，你是努力别停滞。但你还是想能驱动增长、能做点事——"好，我们熬过没死了，因为停滞本质上就是死，所以我们还是在努力别死。"（00:38:58）但第三阶段，你是在跟复杂度作战。这东西会随着时间、在没有外部干预的情况下，把你自己的重量压垮。你总看到这事发生，而且以不同方式显现：一切都越来越复杂，需要更多管理层级、更多人手、更多这更多那，一切更难。利润率……坏事情开始发生，你变慢了。这是最终的——一种更慢的死，因为你规模更大了，但终究还是死。复杂度真的会杀死公司。可能不如别的因素快，但比别的因素都更确定。（00:39:38）所以，种下"简单"的种子永远不嫌早，把它埋进去，让它成为组织文化的一部分。我们就有这么一条文化准则，叫"为简单而战"——字面就是这三个词。我们想传达的信息是："简单值得去争取。"这是第一点，它重要；但另一点是，它得去"争取"。它不会自动发生，而且必然是一场战斗，因为宇宙在跟你作对。捍卫简单要消耗精力，因为万事万物——哪怕是好心的人——都会带来复杂度，因为那才是世界的自然走向。我们想要定价多几档、产品里多几个旋钮拨盘、再多一点……一切都趋向第二定律，熵在增加。总之就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this. The algorithm for seating is a good example of this. Is there any other examples, either in the product or strategy, where you pushed for simplicity and that ended up being right?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢了。那个座位算法就是个好例子。在产品或战略上，还有没有别的你坚持"简单"、结果证明是对的的例子？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: Yeah. So on the product side, in the early years, and Brian gets credit for the actual implementation of this. So we had a relatively broad product, and we can talk about that, pros and cons of that even in the early years, but we were solving for simplicity, and we got this from Apple, we can talk a little bit more about genesis of this, but we had a rule in the HubSpot product as the product grew in those early years that every time you added what we thought of as a knob or dial, called a feature, you had to take one out somewhere else. That's a net amount of... And this is a very coarse measurement. It's like, "Okay, well, not every radio button, checkbox, drop-down, whatever menu item that you put in your nav is necessarily equivalent, but it's better than nothing. It's better than having no constraints. (00:41:27): And so once again, this goes to the binary thing, it's like it just at least forces you to think about it, versus the... The other mistake I think people make in product all the time is that we measure the cost of a feature based on the, usually, or even a new product, based on the cost of implementation. That's the first-order thinking, it's like, "Oh, it's going to take six months to develop, it's going to be Y engineers and Z designers or whatever." Second-order thinking is thinking through the maintenance of that feature. It's like, "Oh, it's not just the first version that goes out, it's like now we have this code base and we have to support and improve or whatever." I get that. The third-order thinking, which I think is the most nuanced, and it turns out to be the most important, is the other costs that complexity adds. (00:42:12): Okay, we'll come back to this. So when you go from product number one to product number two, it's like, "Okay, product number two is going to cost us this much to develop, it's going to have this risk associated with whether it's successful or not, all these things. So there's going to be this carrying cost for product number two." What companies don't think through is that that is... And the maintenance of that, it's like, "Oh, we're going to need a team to maintain that new product." No, what actually happens is that now when you go from product one to two, you have added dimensional complexity to your business. (00:42:43): What I mean by that, it's not an incremental increase like, "Oh, we went from one to two," it's like, now every decision you make has to be made through the lens of, "Now we have two products. We just hired an engineer, do they work on product number one or product number two? We're going to launch a marketing campaign. Do we spend five minutes talking about product number one and two minutes talking about product number two? How do we do anything?" Every chart you look at in terms of the growth, revenue per whatever, it's all of it. Now, every chart that you ever had now has to be sliced by product one and product two in order to really capture that precision. (00:43:14): And so now you have this new dimensional complexity that you just hadn't planned on. And this applies, once again, every level of abstraction. So everything you do in your business should factor in the long-term cost of that complexity. And it should be worth it. Of course, you need, and I can make the case that you need to build product number two and product number N, N plus one over time, but you should be mindful about the cost of that complexity. [inaudible 00:43:39].
turns.zh: 有。产品这边，早些年——具体落地要归功于 Brian。我们产品面其实挺广的，这个可以聊，早年就有它的利弊，但我们是在为简单做优化，而且这思路来自 Apple，它的缘起可以再细说。我们早年有个规矩：随着 HubSpot 产品增长，每当你加一个我们所谓的"旋钮拨盘"（也就是一个功能），你就得在别处拿掉一个。这就是净数量上的……当然这是很粗的测量，就像"哦，不是每个单选钮、复选框、下拉菜单、导航项都等价，但总比没有强，比毫无约束强。"（00:41:27）所以又一次回到二元思路——它至少逼你想一想，而不是……我觉得人在产品上常犯的另一个错是：我们衡量一个功能（甚至一个新产品）的成本，通常只看实现成本。这是一阶思维——"哦，要六个月开发，要 Y 个工程师、Z 个设计师"。二阶思维是想过这功能的维护——"哦，不止第一版上线，而是现在我们有了这个代码库，得持续支持和改进"。这个我懂。三阶思维——我觉得最微妙、结果也最重要——是复杂度带来的其他成本。（00:42:12）好，这个待会儿回来讲。当你从产品一做到产品二，你会想："产品二开发要花这么多，成功与否有这种风险"，各种。所以产品二会有它的持有成本。公司没想透的是：还有它的维护——"哦，我们得派个团队维护新产品。"不，实际发生的是：你从产品一走到产品二，就已经给业务加了"维度复杂度"。（00:42:43）我指的维度复杂度，不是"从一变二"那种增量，而是：现在你每一个决策，都得透过"我们现在有两个产品"这个镜头来做。我们刚招了个工程师，做产品一还是产品二？我们要搞一场营销活动，产品一讲五分钟、产品二讲两分钟？怎么做任何事？你看的每张增长图、每单位收入图，全都是。以前你有的每张图，现在都得按产品一、产品二切开，才能真正看清。（00:43:14）于是你凭空多出一种从没规划过的维度复杂度。这又一次适用于每一层抽象。所以你业务里做的每件事，都该把那复杂度的长期成本算进去。而且它得值。当然你需要——我也能论证你需要随时间去建产品二、产品 N、N+1——但你该对那复杂度的成本保持清醒。（听不清 00:43:39）

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something you've done to help operationalize that? Because I imagine everyone's like, "Yes, this is great. Don't do too many things. Simplify." Hard to do when you're like, "Oh, we got to drive growth. We have this awesome idea, we have this opportunity, we have a competitor." I know that this is part of the culture, so maybe that's the answer, but how do you keep people to actually this principle?
turns.zh: 有没有什么做法帮你把它落地执行？因为我猜大家都会说"对，太好了，别做太多事，做减法。"可真到"哦，我们得驱动增长、我们有个超棒的点子、有个机会、有个竞争对手"的时候，就很难了。我知道这是文化的一部分，所以答案也许就在这——但你是怎么让人真守住这条原则的？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: So it's really hard, I'll say that. And things that have made it easier, it's a little bit idiosyncratic to HubSpot, so part of what has made it easier for us to keep things simple is the early constraints we impose. And we didn't know this at the time. So because we're building for SMB, we have a freemium product. All right, well, when you're doing that, there is literally a limit to how much complexity you can add, because we don't have an army of people that are going to spend in 18 months implementing something. We have to be able to support a product that's free. That's hard to do. It has to be simple enough that someone can get value from this thing. And so there's these self-imposed things. (00:44:41): So the lesson I would carry away is come up with systematic ways and mechanisms, as Amazon would call them, of putting guardrails and constraints in to the degree that you can. Because you can put words on a page and try to infuse it in the culture, it's like, "Oh, we believe in simplicity, we fight for this," and you can have meetings and you can get up in all-hands meetings and reinforce that, which I encourage you to do, but a really, even a reasonably well done system will outbeat any other mechanism that you can try to put it [inaudible 00:45:14]. Those things deteriorate over time. It's hard to scale them. So I'm a big believer in systems and imposed constraints versus-
turns.zh: 说实话这特别难。能让它容易点的东西，有点 HubSpot 的"个性"，所以让我们更容易保持简单的一个原因，是我们早年强加的约束。当时我们并不知道。因为我们做 SMB，有个免费增值产品。好，做这个，你能加的复杂度 literally 是有上限的，因为我们没有一整支大军花 18 个月去实现某个东西。我们得能支撑一个免费产品，那很难。它必须简单到让人能从中获得价值。所以这些是自我强加的限制。（00:44:41）所以我能带走的教训是：想出系统化的方法、机制——像亚马逊说的——去设护栏、加约束，能加多少加多少。因为你可以把话写进文档、注入文化："哦我们相信简单，我们为此而战"，你可以开会、在全员大会上重申——这个我鼓励你做——但哪怕一个做得相当不错的系统，也会胜过你试图放上去的任何其他机制。（听不清 00:45:14）那些东西会随时间退化，很难规模化。所以我极度相信"系统"和"强加的约束"，而不是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can't help but talk about this SMB piece, because I do a lot of angel investing, and classically, companies that focus on small businesses are very challenging, because getting to small businesses at scale is very hard. They're often more old school, not early adopters. You sell one and that's just one small customer, and they're not going to upgrade and roll it out to this large group, and they're not going to increase spend very quickly. For founders that are exploring SMB or trying to win something SMB, any advice other than just, maybe the advice is, "Probably don't do it, it's very hard"?
turns.zh: 我忍不住要聊这个 SMB 话题，因为我做了很多天使投资，而经典看法是：聚焦小企业的公司特别难做，因为规模化地触达小企业非常难。它们往往更老派、不是尝鲜者。你卖一家就是一家小客户，他们不会升级、不会铺开到一大群人，也不会很快增加支出。对那些在探索 SMB、想在小企业市场赢的创始人，除了"也许建议就是：别做，太难了"，还有别的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: No, my advice is absolutely do it.
turns.zh: 不，我的建议是：绝对要做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Great.
turns.zh: 太好了。棒。

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: A, because it's hard, and we'll talk about that, but B, okay, so I'll tell you this quick story in terms of how we chose SMB. And so my co-founder and I met in grad school, and he had done software, he was on the sales and marketing side, I was on the product engineering side, didn't know each other before grad school, and we met there. But one of the things, as we were canoodling on possible ideas of working together on the startup, we said, "Oh," we had done both an enterprise software before, the opposite of opposite of SMB. And there are definitely challenges with enterprise software. One of the biggest one is that life as an enterprise software company sucks as a startup. Sales cycles are super long, feedback loops are super long, you have to have sale, there's all this kind of... You have revenue concentration, which means you don't completely own your product roadmap anymore because whoever's writing the biggest check will ask for these three things and it's really hard to say no, especially as a startup, all these things that go along with that. (00:47:03): It's like, "Okay, we sort of know that game." At the other end of the spectrum, you have consumer startups. It's like, "Okay." The problem with consumer startups is they have very bi-modal outcomes. It's like either you can be super successful, the next Meta, the next Google, the next whatever, or it's going to be to zero. It is very rare that you have, "Oh, you made a few million bucks or whatever." Because either worked, because this is a massive market. The case for SMB is you have almost the best of both worlds. You have the nicety of enterprise, which is, "Oh, I can solve a product and people pay me money for it. I don't have to be advertising subsidized, I don't have this bi-modal outcome. I can build an incrementally more valuable business that's measurable." (00:47:43): So we're "Oh," we went from a 100K in ARR to a million ARR, to 2 million ARR because we're a business software company. But it has the benefit of consumer because there's millions of them out there to sell to, and there is no revenue concentration. You do control your roadmap. You have very short feedback loops. You can try pretty much anything that you want because there's... Like, "Oh, we have 50 customers. If we do this and screw it up, it's like there's 5 million more." Don't intentionally screw it up, but you can experiment, you can take on risks. And by the way, when HubSpot started SMB, it was literally a hundred times harder to succeed in SMB. And we could not raise capital. It was so hard because the common argument was there literally is exactly one company in the history of software that's made a global brand, billions of dollars of market that was into it. No one else had ever created SMB-focused software company before. (00:48:37): And we're like, "Yeah." It's like, "We know." But the nice thing about it is once you figure the physics of it out, because it's so hard to do, you end up, and this has played out, now there's lots more proof points. There's Shopify, there's a bunch of companies that have succeeded in SMB. But one of the things about SMB is that in the software market... By the way, all I know is software. That's the scope of my experience, is that in software, there's what I call reverse gravity. That over time, the market will always pull you up. Because what ends up happening is that smart founders and smart management teams will look at the numbers and say, "Oh, well, as it turns out, our bigger customers stay with us longer, pay us more, often have higher NP, all these things." (00:49:27): And so if you allow yourself to be led by that, which seems like a reasonable, smart thing to do, you will get pulled up in the market. And because of this reverse gravity, almost every company winds up being, every successful software company, ends up being an enterprise software company over the full list of time. That's what you see. The byproduct of that reverse gravity is that every software company ends up being an enterprise software company, so you end up competing with literally everyone. In the SMB world, you're only competing with the people stupid enough to stay focused on SMB, or try to do that. It's a harder thing to accomplish, but once you figure out the physics of it and make it work, it's a much more sustainable, much more fun model. So I encourage, particularly startups, and maybe you fight reverse gravity for some period of time, and maybe... But at least start there, try to make it work, until it gets really, really, really painful, and then try some more. It's like there's just so much value in SMB. It's that idea.
turns.zh: A，因为它难——这个我们待会儿聊；B，好，我给你讲个我们怎么选 SMB 的小故事。我和联合创始人研究生认识的，他做软件、在销售营销侧，我在产品工程侧，上学前不认识。我们琢磨一起创业的点子时，说"哦"，我们俩之前都做过企业级软件，就是 SMB 的反面。企业级软件当然也有挑战，最大的一个是：作为创业公司做企业级软件，日子很难熬。销售周期超长、反馈循环超长，你得有销售团队，各种……还有收入集中——意味着你不再完全掌控产品路线图，因为掏最大支票的人会要那三样东西，你很难拒绝，尤其创业公司，诸如此类。（00:47:03）我们算是"哦，那套游戏我们懂"。光谱另一头是消费级创业。消费级的问题是结果高度两极化：要么超级成功，下一个 Meta、下一个 Google，要么归零。很少有"哦，你就赚了几百万"这种中间态，因为要么成、要么不成，这是个巨大的市场。而 SMB 的妙处在于几乎是两全其美：有企业级的惬意——"哦，我能做个产品，人家付钱给我，不用靠广告补贴，没有这种两极化结果，我能建立一门可度量、逐步增值的生意。"（00:47:43）所以我们就"哦"，从 10 万 ARR 到 100 万、再到 200 万 ARR，因为我们是商业软件公司。但它又有消费级的优势：外面有几百万家可卖，没有收入集中，你掌控路线图，反馈循环极短。你几乎能试任何东西——"哦，我们有 50 个客户，这事儿搞砸了，外面还有 500 万呢。"别故意搞砸，但你能做实验、能冒险。而且，HubSpot 起步做 SMB 时，成功的难度 literally 是现在的上百倍。我们也融不到钱，因为常见的论点是：软件史上 exactly 只有一家公司做成了面向 SMB 的全球品牌、几十亿的市场。之前从没人做成过 SMB 导向的软件公司。（00:48:37）我们说"是啊，我们知道。"但它的好处是：一旦你搞清了它的"物理规律"——因为它太难了——你就能站稳，而事实也证明了这点，现在成功的佐证多多了，有 Shopify，有一批 SMB 成功的公司。但 SMB 在软件市场里有个特点……顺便，我只懂软件，这是我的经验范围。软件里有所谓"反重力"：随着时间推移，市场总会把你往上拉。因为聪明创始人和管理团队会看数字说："哦，结果我们的更大客户留得更久、付得更多、往往 NPS 更高"，各种。（00:49:27）所以如果你任由自己被这牵引——这看起来合理又聪明——你就会被市场往上拉。因为这反重力，几乎每家公司，每家成功的软件公司，最终都变成企业级软件公司。你看到的就这个。反重力的副产品是：每家公司最终都成了企业级软件公司，于是你等于在跟所有人竞争。而在 SMB 世界里，你只跟那些"傻到"坚持聚焦 SMB、或试图做这事的人竞争。它更难做成，但一旦你搞清物理规律、让它跑通，它就是更可持续、更有意思的模式。所以我鼓励——尤其创业公司——也许你跟反重力对抗一阵，也许……但至少从那儿起步，努力让它跑通，直到真的真的真的痛了，再试试别的。SMB 里的价值就这么多。就是这意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so this theme has come up a bunch already in our conversation. I asked Chris Miller, previous podcast guest, what you're amazing at and what I should talk to you about. And he said that you're very good at zigging when other people are zagging, and zagging when other people are zigging. And I think that's already come across in our conversation. I guess, is there anything else along those lines that you think might be helpful to people, in terms of how you think about that, or examples of that in action?
turns.zh: 好，这个主题咱们聊里已经冒出来好几次了。我问过上一期嘉宾 Chris Miller，你擅长什么、我该跟你聊什么。他说你特别擅长"别人往东你往西、别人往西你往东"。我觉得这点在咱们对话里已经显现了。这方面还有没有别的、你觉得可能对人有帮助的思路或实际例子？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: So this comes down to high-conviction, low-consensus bets. And so we had like three things that we were zigging... And by the way, it's not just me. My co-founder and I both have that zig versus zag. And we ask ourselves this to this day, it's like, "Okay, well we understand this is the way the world moves, this is the way it's normally done, but have we considered this completely? And I'm not saying we should do it, but have we considered this alternate path?" So I would encourage you, at any stage of the company, you don't necessarily have to do the zig versus zag, but you should at least know what the zig would've been and have talked it through. So that's thing number one. (00:51:29): Some of the best startup advice I've heard and I've ever given is, "Startups should focus on one thing and be really, really exceptionally world-class better than anyone else at that one thing." And one of our early zigs is, "We are going to do exactly the opposite of that." So from year one, HubSpot decided to build an SEO tool, web analytics, blogging tool, content management, all of it. And every one of those categories that we were building a product in, literally this is year one, had great products with great companies behind them. And so it's like, "Okay, well, why would you do that?" And-
turns.zh: 这就回到"高信念、低共识的赌注"。我们有三件事是在"往西"。顺便，这不只我一个人，我和联合创始人都这样"逆向"。直到今天我们还问自己："好，我们理解世界通常这么走、通常这么做，但我们真把替代路径想透了吗？我不是说就该那么做，但我们有没有考虑过那条岔路？"所以我鼓励你：公司任何阶段，不一定要真去逆向，但至少该知道"顺向"会是什么、并把它聊透。这是第一点。（00:51:29）我听过、也给过的最好的创业建议之一是："创业公司该聚焦一件事，在那一件事上做到世界级、比别人强一大截。"而我们早期的一个逆向是："我们偏要正好反着来。"所以从第一年起，HubSpot 就决定做 SEO 工具、网站分析、博客工具、内容管理，全做。而且我们进的每个品类——真的是第一年——背后都有很棒的产品、很棒的公司。所以就像"哦，你干嘛这么做？"于是——

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: And so it's like, okay, well why would you do that? And the reason is that the one thing we wanted to be good at was solving for the actual customer problem that existed, and the customer problem that existed was not a dearth of tools, lots of great SEO blogging, everything, all the tools existed, but SMB specifically did not have the wherewithal to put all those pieces together. So you and I, it's like, "Oh, I can throw a website up. I can put Google Analytics on it. I can put a Wufoo Typeform format. I can do all these things. I can wire doc. No big deal. Why is this so hard?" But for most people, most SMBs, that's a science project, and so we said, okay, in order for us to solve the actual customer problem, we have to solve the actual customer problem, even if it's uncomfortable, even though it's contrarian and every instinct and every advice we've heard or given says we should not do this. We should not go that broad. (00:52:53): But once we make that decision so that the other lesson learned, it's like, and we said this in the early years and it's gotten better since, let's say you do this, and this is the all-in-one approach, we're going to have this broad-based product. It's like, "Okay, we're going to be many miles wide and only so inches deep." One of these, and this goes back to our very systematic thinking, is like, "Okay, we're going to measure each of those individual product categories that we're now playing in. Are we in the top three in the market in that category? If the answer is yes, that means we invested too much in that category." We should not be in the top three because our value proposition is not that we are the top three blogging tools or one of the top three web analytics tools. We have the top three, whatever, our value proposition is that everything works so well together that that being in the top three and having those right features or whatever doesn't matter. (00:53:41): Doesn't matter as much as the all-in-one. And that means we over-index on one individual category by virtue. That was one of our heuristics for being able to tell that we were over-indexed on one particular aspect of it.
turns.zh: 于是就像，好，你干嘛这么做？原因是：我们想做好的那"一件事"，是解决真实存在的客户问题；而那个问题不是缺工具——各种好 SEO、好博客工具都有，全都有——但 SMB 特别没有能力把那些拼在一起。你和我，"哦，我搭个网站、挂上 Google Analytics、放个 Wufoo/Typeform 表单、接个文档，小意思，怎么这么难？"但对大多数人、大多数 SMB，那是个科学项目。所以我们说：好，要真正解决客户问题，就得解决那真实问题，哪怕不舒服、哪怕反共识、哪怕我们听到和给过的每条本能和建议都说不该这么干。我们不该铺那么广。（00:52:53）但一旦我们做了那决定，另一个教训就来了——早年我们就这么说，后来更好了——假设你这么做，也就是"一体化"路线，我们要做广覆盖的产品。就像"好，我们要好几英里宽、却只这么几英寸深。"其中一点，又回到我们那套系统化思维：我们会衡量现在涉足的每个品类——"我们在这个品类里市场排前三吗？如果是，说明我们在这个品类投太多了。"我们不该排前三，因为我们的价值主张不是"我们是前三的博客工具"或"前三的网站分析工具"。前三什么的，我们的价值主张是：所有东西配合得那么好，以至于排不排前三、有没有那些功能根本不重要。（00:53:41）一体化比那重要得多。这意味着我们若在某个单品类上过度投入，就说明过头了。这是我们用来判断"在某个单点上押太重"的一条启发式规则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is hilarious. Rarely do I hear we're in the top three and we're doing the wrong thing. We are too good at this.
turns.zh: 太好笑了。我很少听到"我们排前三，说明我们做错了，是我们在这上面太强了"。

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: And by the way, and we changed that over time in the startup world, and now I would argue that most of the categories we play in, we are, as the surveys would tell you that we're in the top three in each of those categories now, but at the time when we are very, very resource constrained, we were trying to be disciplined and focused.
turns.zh: 顺便说，后来我们在创业圈里改了这点；现在我会说，我们涉足的大多数品类，按调查你都会看到我们如今在每个品类都排前三了。但当时我们资源极度受限，是在努力保持纪律和聚焦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're just racking up all these very contrarian approaches to company building. I imagine people listening to this might feel like, "Okay, cool, I'm just going to build a bunch of stuff. This is great. I worked for HubSpot." Do you have any heuristics for when it makes sense to go wide and not deep that you share with founders? When do you think it makes sense versus now you should actually follow the common advice here?
turns.zh: 我们这一路攒了一堆特别反共识的建公司方法。我猜听的人可能会觉得"好，酷，那我就啥都造一点，太棒了，我给 HubSpot 干过"。你有没有什么启发式，告诉创始人什么时候该"铺广而不是做深"？你觉得什么时候合适、什么时候其实该听那条常规建议？

turns.speaker: Dharmesh Shah
turns.en: Yeah, so it comes down to what problem you're solving. So I think one of the mistakes I think founders make is that, especially product oriented founders, is that we fall in love with the solution instead of falling in love with the actual problem, and you need to fall in love with the problem and putting that constraint on yourself forces you to understand and at least label and define what problem you're solving because oftentimes we can describe our product or whatever, but we struggle sometimes as founders to describe the actual problem. So if you can make the case, which HubSpot did, it's like, okay, it's not like we immediately jump to that like, "Oh, we have this epiphany. We're going to build the all-in-one, do all the things kind of thing." We're like, "Oh, in actually talking to customers", we considered doing it like, "Oh, we'll just do this marketing piece." (00:55:27): We'll just do this or whatever. It's like, no, that's not their issue, their issues it's not that these things don't exist, so if you, as a result of talking to customers and understanding the problem deeply, you come to the conclusion that you need to do more than just one thing, but then you should force yourself to have a discipline that we did, which is, here's why we're going to go a little bit broad, and here's how we're going to make sure that that broadness doesn't kill us. You have to have the self-imposed constraint. You can't have the best of both worlds. You can't say, " We're going to be all in one, and oh, by the way, we're going to be the best." No, you can't be the best. You can say, we solve this particular problem the best, but we're not going to have the best product along any of those dimensions.
turns.zh: 有，关键看你解决的是什么问题。我觉得创始人——尤其产品型创始人——常犯的一个错是爱上方案，而不是爱上真实的问题。你得爱上问题；给自己加这个约束，会逼你去理解、至少去标注和定义你到底在解决什么问题，因为我们常常能描述自己的产品，却往往在描述真实问题上有困难。所以如果你能像 HubSpot 那样论证："哦，我们不是立刻就跳到'我们要做一体化、啥都做'那种灵光一现。"我们是"哦，真去跟客户聊"时，也考虑过"哦，我们就只做营销那块"，或者只做这个那个。不，那不是他们的问题——他们的问题不是这些工具不存在。所以如果你通过跟客户深聊、深刻理解问题，得出结论说你需要做的比"一件事"多，那你就该强迫自己像我们那样有纪律：这是我们要稍微铺广的理由，以及我们怎么确保这铺广不会害死我们。你必须有自我强加的约束。你不能两全其美。你不能说"我们要做一体化，哦顺便，我们还要做到最好。"不，你做不到最好。你可以说"我们把这个特定问题解得最好"，但你不可能在任何一个维度上都有最好的产品。（00:55:27）
